title: Phase-Locked Loops
intro: A phase-locked loop is a feedback system that compares phases instead of voltages. It makes an oscillator's phase follow a reference, which lets a chip multiply clock frequencies exactly, synthesize carriers, remove clock skew and clean up jitter (Razavi, Chapter 16).

items: A VCO's phase can only be changed by changing its frequency for a while, because phase is the integral of frequency.
A phase detector measures the phase error and, through a filter, nudges the VCO's control voltage until the error stops changing.
Locked means the phase difference is constant, so the output frequency equals the input frequency exactly (or exactly $M$ times it with a divider).

blocks.alt: Block diagram of a charge-pump phase-locked loop. The reference frequency enters a phase detector, followed by a charge pump, a loop filter and a voltage-controlled oscillator. The oscillator output is the loop output and also goes through a divide-by-N block back to the second input of the phase detector.
blocks.caption: The modern charge-pump PLL with a feedback divider.

blocks.text: Choosing a design? The PLL Building Blocks chapter that follows compares PFD, charge-pump, loop-filter and VCO circuits in depth, with noise and spur estimates and an architecture selection guide.

A PLL's 'error amplifier' only understands phase: the phase detector converts phase to voltage and the VCO converts voltage back to phase. Keep track of those unit changes and the loop algebra is ordinary feedback theory.

blocks.title: Why lock phase at all?
blocks.text: Two loops both aim to make an output clock's frequency equal a reference: one compares frequencies, the other compares phases. Why does only the second give an exactly equal frequency?
solution: A frequency-comparing loop behaves like a unity-gain amplifier with offset: mismatch in the detector leaves a small but finite frequency error, and over many cycles the two clocks drift apart.

A phase-comparing loop is locked only if the phase difference stays constant; any frequency difference, however small, would make the phase error grow without bound. So in lock the frequencies are identical.
blocks.answer: Phase lock forces zero average frequency error; frequency lock leaves a residual error.
